title: Feminist and womanist voices
hookLine: women theologians reread scripture and tradition, recovering women's voices

cards: A servant woman runs into the desert. She's pregnant, she's been treated harshly, and she has nowhere to go. Her name is Hagar, an Egyptian in the household of Abraham and Sarah, and this path has met her before.
By a spring of water in the wilderness, the angel of the Lord finds her and speaks to her by name. Then Hagar does something startling. She gives God a name: "Thou God seest me."
Her story can be read as a side scene in Abraham's. Some theologians read it as the main one.

teach.b: Feminist theology is a name for rereading scripture and the Christian past with women in view. It asks: who is speaking here? Who is silent?
Who got left out of the retelling? Scholars such as Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Rosemary Radford Ruether wrote in this way.
Womanist theology grew from the experience of Black women, taking its name from a word used by the writer Alice Walker.

One womanist theologian, Delores Williams, read Hagar as a mirror: a woman enslaved, used, and sent into the wilderness, and met there by God, who doesn't free her right away but helps her and her child survive.
Read this way, women turn up at turning points. In Mark, when the disciples have fled, women are watching the cross from a distance.
In John, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus in the garden and goes to tell the disciples she has seen the Lord.

Paul commends a woman he calls, in the King James spelling, Phebe, "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," and sends greetings to women who worked alongside him. None of this is hidden; it's on the page.
Traditions differ on what these texts mean for leadership, ordination and roles.
Some churches ordain women as pastors and priests; others hold that certain ministries belong to men. The method is open to anyone: read slowly, and ask whose story is also here.

how: Some Christians study the women of the Bible in reading groups and sermon series, and feminist and womanist theology is taught in some seminaries; churches differ on whether women are ordained.

games.q: you're Hagar, alone by a spring in the wilderness. the angel of the Lord has just spoken to you by name. what do you do?
games.why: Hagar names the God who spoke to her: "Thou God seest me." the outcast in the wilderness is the one who names God.

practice: Bring Hagar to mind, alone by the spring, carrying fear, exhaustion and a child on the way; hear a voice call her by name, and hear her answer, naming God as the one who sees her.

If you pray, you can speak to the God who sees; if you don't, notice who in your own life goes unseen. And if you're the one being hurt or unsafe right now, please reach local emergency help, or call or text 988 in the US.

wordCard.voice: Feminist and womanist voices. Women's rereadings of scripture and tradition, recovering stories like Hagar's, and the women at the cross and the empty tomb.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 16:13: a God of seeing. Hagar's name for God; the King James renders it "Thou God seest me."
